pastel.etymology_derivation: Late Latin pasta ('dough, paste') gives English 'pastry' and Spanish pastel. A cognate on the table.

café.etymology_derivation: Turkish kahve → Italian caffè → Spanish café. An international word shared across Europe.

querer.etymology_derivation: Latin quaerere ('to seek, ask for') evolved in Spanish to 'to want' and 'to love'. When you make an inquiry in English, you are asking what you want.

tú.etymology_derivation: Latin tū — the ancient Indo-European second person singular, preserved in Shakespeare's thou.

yo.etymology_derivation: Latin egō → eo → yo. English 'I' descends from Proto-Germanic *ik, born from the very same ancestral stem.

el.etymology_derivation: Latin demonstrative ille ('that one') trimmed down over centuries to el. Spanish pointers became articles.

la.etymology_derivation: Latin illa → la. It functions as both the feminine definite article ('the') and the direct object pronoun ('her / it').

lo.etymology_derivation: Latin illum → lo. Walks one step to the left of conjugated verbs: I it want.

un_poco.etymology_derivation: Latin paucus ('few, little') gives English 'paucity' and Spanish poco.

colección.etymology_derivation: Latin collectiōnem. The -CIÓN ending is your passport: thousands of words convert, and every one takes la.

tradición.etymology_derivation: Latin trāditiō ('a surrender, handing over') — tradition is knowledge handed across generations.

confirmación.etymology_derivation: Latin confirmātiō. Accent on the ó marks the stressed final syllable.

organización.etymology_derivation: Latin organizātiō. Spanish spells with z where British English uses s.

opinión.etymology_derivation: Latin opīniō. Like -ción, words in -sión and -ión are consistently feminine.

reservación.etymology_derivation: Latin reservātiō. Also heard as la reserva in Spain.

complicación.etymology_derivation: Latin complicātiō, from con- ('together') + plicāre ('to fold'). A complication is literally an entanglement of folds.

pasión.etymology_derivation: Latin passiō ('suffering, enduring'). Passion is what stirs the spirit so deeply one suffers for it.

invitación.etymology_derivation: Latin invītātiō. The -ción ending guarantees feminine gender: la invitación.

decisión.etymology_derivation: Latin dēcīsiō ('a cutting off'). Making a decision is cutting away other options.

confirmar.etymology_derivation: confirmación → confirmar. Strip -ación, attach -ar. One rule turns hundreds of nouns into verbs.

organizar.context_translation: I want to organize the party.
organizar.etymology_derivation: organización → organizar. The infinitive in -ar is stressed on the final syllable.

celebrar.etymology_derivation: celebración → celebrar. The trap: not *celebratar. Strip the whole -ación before adding -ar.

participar.context_translation: I want to participate a little.
participar.etymology_derivation: participación → participar. Sounds everyday in Spanish, whereas 'participate' sounds formal in English.

visitar.etymology_derivation: visitation → visitar. No preposition 'to' needed in Spanish: quiero visitar (two words where English needs three).

invitar.etymology_derivation: invitación → invitar. Pronouns hook onto the infinitive: quiero invitarlo ('I want to invite him/it').

reservar.context_translation: I want to reserve a table.

preparar.context_translation: I want to prepare the coffee.
preparar.etymology_derivation: preparación → preparar. Latin praeparāre ('to make ready beforehand').

considerar.context_translation: I want to consider the option.
considerar.etymology_derivation: consideración → considerar. From Latin considerāre, originally 'to observe the stars together'.

no.etymology_derivation: Latin nōn → Spanish no. Negation in Spanish is beautifully direct: place no right before the verb cluster.

nada.context_translation: I want nothing (I don't want anything).
nada.etymology_derivation: Latin rēs nāta ('born thing'). In Spanish, double negation reinforces: no quiero nada.

ser.etymology_derivation: Ser describes what something is: identity, origin, inherent nature. Latin esse fused with sedēre ('to sit/settle').

estar.etymology_derivation: Latin stāre ('to stand') gives English 'stand' and 'state'. Estar describes how or where something stands right now.

es.shift_rule: Latin est — identical to English is
es.etymology_derivation: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ésti → Latin est → Spanish es. Sibling to English is.

está.etymology_derivation: Latin stat ('he/she stands') → está. Accent on the á keeps the stress on the tail.

estás.context_translation: How are you? (How do you stand?)

muy.etymology_derivation: Latin multum ('much') clipped to muy before adjectives and adverbs.

bueno.etymology_derivation: Latin bonus gives English 'bonus' and Spanish bueno (o diphthongizes to ue under stress).

buena.etymology_derivation: Feminine agreement in -a: la tradición es buena.

contento.etymology_derivation: Latin contentus ('contained, satisfied'). Paired with estar for emotional states.

contenta.etymology_derivation: Feminine agreement: changes -o to -a when describing a woman.

universidad.etymology_derivation: Latin universitātem → universidad. English -ty is Spanish -dad, and every -dad noun is feminine.

ciudad.etymology_derivation: Latin cīvitātem ('citizenship, city') gives English 'city' and 'civic', and Spanish ciudad.

verdad.etymology_derivation: Latin vēritātem gives English 'verity' and Spanish verdad.

exactamente.etymology_derivation: Latin ablative exactā mente ('with an exact mind') fused into a single adverb suffix.

naturalmente.etymology_derivation: natural + mente. When the adjective doesn't end in -o, it attaches directly.

rápidamente.etymology_derivation: rápida + mente. Keeps the accent on rá- even though the suffix is stressed.

dónde.etymology_derivation: Latin dē + unde ('from where') → dónde. Carries written accent in questions.

qué.etymology_derivation: Latin quid → qué. Stressed in questions (accented qué), unstressed as conjunction (que).

porque.etymology_derivation: One word without accent when answering: porque quiero.

allí.etymology_derivation: Latin eccum illīc ('behold there') → allí. Accent marks the final stress.

mágico.etymology_derivation: Greek magikos → Latin magicus → mágico. All words in -ico carry an antepenultimate accent.

natural.etymology_derivation: Latin nātūrālis. Words in -al have identical singular spelling in English and Spanish.

hola.etymology_derivation: H is completely silent in Spanish. Cognate with English hallo/hullo.

gracias.etymology_derivation: Latin grātia ('favor, grace'). Spanish thanks are plural: 'graces to you'.

adiós.etymology_derivation: a ('to') + Dios ('God') — identical to French adieu: 'I commend you to God'.

usted.etymology_derivation: Vuestra Merced ('Your Mercy') worn down over centuries to usted. Takes 3rd-person verb forms.

tener.etymology_derivation: Latin tenēre ('to hold'). While other tongues used 'have' (like French avoir), Spanish promoted 'hold' (tener) to main possession.

tengo.etymology_derivation: Latin teneō developed an epenthetic velar g: tengo.

tienes.etymology_derivation: Stem vowel e diphthongizes to ie when stressed: tienes.

hay.etymology_derivation: Latin habet ('it has') + Old Spanish y ('there', Latin ibi). Identical structure to French il y a.

casa.etymology_derivation: Latin casa originally meant a cottage, replacing domus in everyday Romance speech.

hotel.etymology_derivation: Silent initial H. Latin hospitāle gives both 'hospital' and 'hotel'.

azul.etymology_derivation: Hispano-Arabic lāzaward ('lapis lazuli') → azul. English azure is the exact same word.

rojo.etymology_derivation: Latin russeus ('reddish') → rojo. Cognate with English russet and ruby.

grande.etymology_derivation: Latin grandis. Invariable for gender: el hotel grande, la casa grande.

pequeño.etymology_derivation: Romance root *pikk- expressing smallness. Feminine is pequeña.

buenos_días.etymology_derivation: Día is masculine (el día, from Latin diēs) despite ending in -a: buenos días.

buenas_noches.etymology_derivation: Latin noctem shows the regular Spanish sound shift: -ct- becomes -ch-.

llamar.context_translation: What's your name? (How do you call yourself?)
llamar.etymology_derivation: Latin clāmāre ('to call, shout') shifted initial cl- to ll-. Me llamo = 'I call myself'.

me_llamo.english_meaning: my name is (lit. I call myself)
me_llamo.etymology_derivation: Spanish introduces by reflexive verb: me llamo ('I call myself').

cómo.etymology_derivation: Latin quō modō ('by what measure/way') → cómo. Accented in questions.

letra.context_translation: With what letter does it start?
letra.etymology_derivation: Latin littera. Double t simplified to single t in Spanish.

pan.etymology_derivation: Latin pānis gives English 'pantry' (where bread is kept) and 'companion' (one with whom you break bread).

vino.etymology_derivation: Latin vīnum. Spanish v is pronounced as a soft bilabial /b/ or /β/.

agua.shift_rule: Latin aqua (takes el in singular for phonetics)
agua.context_translation: I want a glass of water.
agua.etymology_derivation: Feminine noun (las aguas) that takes el in the singular to prevent a collision with stressed initial /a/.

noche.etymology_derivation: Latin noctem. The -ct- became Spanish -ch-: octō → ocho, lactem → leche.

leche.etymology_derivation: Latin lactem → leche. English keeps the Latin root in lactose and lactate.

llave.etymology_derivation: Latin clāvis ('key') gives English 'clavicle' (little key bone) and Spanish llave.

hacer.context_translation: I want to make a reservation.
hacer.etymology_derivation: Latin facere shifted initial f- to silent h- in Spanish: hacer. English keeps the f in fact and factory.

hijo.etymology_derivation: Latin fīlius gives English 'filial' and Spanish hijo (initial f- silenced to h-).

actualmente.etymology_derivation: Latin actuālis ('pertaining to acts/now'). Spanish narrowed it to time ('currently'); English to reality ('actually' = en realidad).

librería.context_phrase: Compré el libro en la librería.
librería.context_translation: I bought the book at the bookstore.
librería.etymology_derivation: Latin librāria ('bookstall'). La librería sells books; la biblioteca lends them.

éxito.etymology_derivation: Latin exitus ('outcome'). Spanish focused on the triumphant outcome; English on the physical doorway (la salida).

asistir.context_translation: I want to attend the meeting.
asistir.etymology_derivation: Latin assistō ('to stand by'). Spanish kept 'standing by as spectator' (asistir a); helping is ayudar.

recordar.context_translation: I want to remember the moment.
recordar.etymology_derivation: Latin recordārī ('to call back to the heart'). Recording audio is grabar.

sensible.context_translation: He is a very sensitive person.
sensible.etymology_derivation: Latin sensibilis ('feeling deeply'). The sensible, prudent person is sensato.

sopa.etymology_derivation: Germanic *supa gives English soup and Spanish sopa. Soap is el jabón.

embarazada.etymology_derivation: From Portuguese/Spanish embarazar ('to encumber'). Embarrassed is avergonzado/a.

hablar.english_meaning: to speak, to talk (hablo: I speak)
hablar.etymology_derivation: Latin fabulārī (to converse, tell stories — English fable and fabulous) shifted initial f- to silent h-: hablar!

mesa.context_translation: I want to reserve a table.
mesa.etymology_derivation: Latin mēnsa ('table') gave Spanish la mesa — which English borrowed in the American Southwest for a flat-topped 'table' mountain!

desear.etymology_derivation: Climb the English register ladder from 'want' to 'desire' and Spanish desear is waiting.

entrar.context_translation: I want to go in here.
entrar.etymology_derivation: Trade phrasal 'go in' for formal 'enter' → entrar (used with en: entrar en la casa).

preferir.etymology_derivation: Stem-changing e → ie in the boot: prefiero, prefieres, prefiere.

importante.etymology_derivation: Adjectives ending in -e do not change for gender: el punto importante, la idea importante.

diferente.etymology_derivation: Invariable for gender in the singular.

posible.etymology_derivation: Spanish simplifies double ss to single s: posible, imposible.

imposible.etymology_derivation: in- becomes im- before p: imposible.

terminar.context_translation: I want to finish the work.
terminar.etymology_derivation: English 'terminate' sounds like a robot; Spanish terminar is the everyday word for 'finish'!

comer.etymology_derivation: Latin com- ('completely') + edere ('to eat', cousin of English edible and eat).

beber.etymology_derivation: Latin bibere — English imbibe and beverage.

vivir.etymology_derivation: Latin vīvere — English vivid, revive, survive.

abrir.etymology_derivation: Latin aperīre ('to uncover/open') — English aperture and aperitif!

nunca.etymology_derivation: Can stand before the verb alone (Nunca voy) or after no + verb (No voy nunca).

nadie.etymology_derivation: Reinforces no in Spanish double negation.

soy.etymology_derivation: Ends in -oy like estoy, voy, doy!

estamos.etymology_derivation: Takes no accent mark because stress falls naturally on -ta-.

caliente.shift_rule: Used with estar for food/drink temperature

frío.etymology_derivation: Notice feminine fría agrees with el agua!

listo.shift_rule: Chameleon adjective: es listo vs. está listo
listo.etymology_derivation: With ser, ser listo means 'to be clever/sharp'; with estar, estar listo means 'to be ready'!

aburrido.shift_rule: Chameleon adjective: es aburrido vs. está aburrido
aburrido.context_phrase: La película es aburrida y estoy aburrido.
aburrido.context_translation: The movie is boring and I am bored.
aburrido.etymology_derivation: English uses -ing vs. -ed (boring vs. bored); Spanish uses ser vs. estar!

rico.shift_rule: Chameleon adjective: es rico vs. está rico
rico.etymology_derivation: es rico = 'he is wealthy'; está rico = 'this food tastes delicious'!

seguro.shift_rule: Chameleon adjective: es seguro vs. está seguro
seguro.etymology_derivation: es seguro = 'it is safe'; estoy seguro = 'I am sure/certain'.

quién.etymology_derivation: Has a plural form quiénes when asking about multiple people!

cuándo.etymology_derivation: Accented in direct and indirect questions.

cuánto.etymology_derivation: Agrees in gender and number when before a noun (¿Cuántos años tienes?).

cuál.etymology_derivation: Used before es for 'What is [your name/problem/option]?' when selecting an identifier.

económico.etymology_derivation: Always accented on the third-from-last syllable.

señor.etymology_derivation: Latin senior ('older') — English senior and sire.

señora.etymology_derivation: Takes el/la when talking ABOUT them (el señor García), and no article when addressing them directly.

mucho.context_translation: Thank you very much (lit. Many graces).
mucho.etymology_derivation: muy ('very') goes before adjectives/adverbs; mucho/a/os/as goes with verbs and nouns!

tiene.etymology_derivation: Stem change e → ie under stress.

tenemos.shift_rule: 1st person plural of tener (outside the boot!)
tenemos.etymology_derivation: Because the stress moves onto the ending (-ne-mos), the stem vowel e stays unchanged!

tienen.etymology_derivation: Stress lands on the stem, so e splits into ie: tienen.

problema.etymology_derivation: Greek nouns ending in -ma (el problema, el sistema, el programa, el tema, el clima) are MASCULINE despite ending in -a!

tiempo.etymology_derivation: Covers both clock/calendar time and the weather.

poder.english_meaning: to be able to, can (puedo: I can)
poder.shift_rule: Boot verb o → ue (puedo, puedes, puede, podemos)
poder.etymology_derivation: Vulgar Latin *potēre — root of potent and potential.

puedo.english_meaning: I can, I am able to
puedo.etymology_derivation: o splits into ue under stress.

puedes.etymology_derivation: Chains directly with a bare infinitive.

dormir.etymology_derivation: Latin dormīre — English dormitory and dormant.

empezar.english_meaning: to begin, to start (empiezo: I start)
empezar.shift_rule: Boot verb e → ie (takes a before infinitive)
empezar.context_phrase: La clase empieza a las nueve.
empezar.etymology_derivation: Takes a before a following infinitive: empiezo a comprender ('I'm starting to understand').

pedir.english_meaning: to ask for, to order (pido: I order/ask for)
pedir.shift_rule: Boot verb e → i (pido, pides, pide, pedimos)
pedir.context_translation: I want to order a coffee.
pedir.etymology_derivation: Latin petere ('to seek/ask for') — English petition and appetite. Needs no 'for'!

verde.etymology_derivation: Ends in -e, so masculine and feminine are identical.

hermoso.etymology_derivation: Latin formōsus ('finely formed') — initial f- became silent h-: hermoso!

pesadilla.etymology_derivation: pesado ('heavy', cousin of peso/pensive) + -illa = 'the heavy little thing on your chest in sleep'!

limón.etymology_derivation: In Spanish, la lima is the smaller green lime, and el limón (-ón augmentative) is the larger yellow lemon!

poquito.english_meaning: a tiny bit, a little bit
poquito.context_phrase: Un poquito de agua, por favor.
poquito.context_translation: A little bit of water, please.
poquito.etymology_derivation: poco + -ito changes c to qu to keep the /k/ sound: poquito.

ir.context_translation: I am going to go tomorrow.
ir.etymology_derivation: Latin īre ('to go', preserved in English exit 'go out' and transit 'go across')!

voy.context_translation: I am going to visit Madrid.
voy.etymology_derivation: Followed by a + infinitive, voy a expresses the near future.

vamos.english_meaning: we go, we are going; let's go!
vamos.etymology_derivation: Used both for 'we go' and standalone 'Let's go!'

van.context_translation: They are going to arrive late.

mañana.context_translation: Tomorrow I am going to work.
mañana.etymology_derivation: As an adverb (mañana) it means 'tomorrow'; as a feminine noun (la mañana) it means 'the morning' (mañana por la mañana = 'tomorrow morning')!

hoy.etymology_derivation: Latin hodiē lost its middle d and became hoy (the exact cousin of the -hui in French aujourd'hui!).

ver.context_translation: I am going to see it/him today.
ver.etymology_derivation: Pronouns can hook directly onto the tail of the infinitive: verlo ('to see it/him')!

comprar.etymology_derivation: Latin comparāre ('to get ready, purchase') — English compare.

para.english_meaning: for (recipient, destination, deadline), in order to
para.etymology_derivation: Old Spanish pora (por + a) — think of para as a forward arrow pointing at the recipient, destination, deadline, or goal ('in order to').

por.english_meaning: for (because of, in exchange for, duration), through, by
por.etymology_derivation: Latin prō + per — think of por as the cause behind an action, the price on a scale, or a path through space/time.

con.english_meaning: with (conmigo: with me, contigo: with you)
con.etymology_derivation: Latin cum — the prefix in connect, combine, companion.

sin.etymology_derivation: Followed by a bare infinitive, sin means 'without [doing]-ing': sin decir nada ('without saying anything').

en.context_phrase: Vivo en Madrid y el libro está en la mesa.
en.context_translation: I live in Madrid and the book is on the table.
en.etymology_derivation: One Spanish preposition covers 'in' (en la casa), 'on' (en la mesa), and 'at' (en el hotel)!

de.context_translation: I am coming from the hotel.
de.etymology_derivation: Fuses with masculine singular article el into del ('of the / from the').

a.english_meaning: to, at (a + el = al; also personal 'a')
a.context_translation: I am going to the restaurant.
a.etymology_derivation: Fuses with masculine singular article el into al ('to the / at the').

regalo.context_phrase: Es un regalo para mi madre.
regalo.context_translation: It is a gift for my mother.
regalo.etymology_derivation: English 'regale' comes from the same root.

mi.shift_rule: Agrees in number with the possession
mi.context_phrase: Es mi amigo y ellos son mis amigos.
mi.context_translation: He is my friend and they are my friends.
mi.etymology_derivation: Unstressed mi (no accent) means 'my'; accented mí (after a preposition: para mí) means 'me'!

tu_poss.shift_rule: No accent on possessive tu ('your') vs. accented tú ('you')

su.english_meaning: his, her, its, your (usted), their (plural: sus)
su.shift_rule: Agrees in number with the thing owned (su / sus)
su.context_translation: María is looking for her brother.
su.etymology_derivation: Only changes for singular (su libro) vs. plural (sus libros) — never for gender!

nuestro.english_meaning: our (agrees in gender and number: nuestro/a/os/as)
nuestro.etymology_derivation: Unlike mi/tu/su, nuestro agrees in both gender and number: nuestro padre, nuestra madre.

padre.etymology_derivation: Plural los padres means 'the parents' (mother and father together).

hermano.context_phrase: Tengo un hermano y una hermana.
hermano.context_translation: I have a brother and a sister.
hermano.etymology_derivation: Latin germānus ('of the same seed/parents', English 'germane') lost its initial g- in Spanish: hermano!

este.context_phrase: Quiero este libro y esta mesa.
este.context_translation: I want this book and this table.
este.etymology_derivation: Zone 1 (near me, aquí): este (m.), esta (f.), esto (neuter idea).

ese.context_translation: Do you want that coffee (near you)?
ese.etymology_derivation: Zone 2 (near you, ahí): ese (m.), esa (f.), eso ('that thing/idea').

aquel.shift_rule: Zone 3 demonstrative (allí: far away in space or time)
aquel.context_phrase: Aquella casa allí es muy antigua.
aquel.context_translation: That house over there is very old.
aquel.etymology_derivation: Zone 3 (far from both of us, allí): aquel (m.), aquella (f.).

uno.english_meaning: one (un before m. noun, una before f. noun)
uno.etymology_derivation: Drops -o before a masculine noun: un libro.

tres.etymology_derivation: Shared Indo-European root with English three.

nueve.etymology_derivation: Latin novem diphthongized o → ue (just like nuevo 'new'!).

treinta.etymology_derivation: Numbers 31–99 join with y ('and'): treinta y uno.

cien.etymology_derivation: Bare cien before a noun (cien años) or alone; ciento before 1–99 (ciento dos).

año.english_meaning: year (tener X años: to be X years old)
año.context_translation: I am thirty years old (lit. I have thirty years).
año.etymology_derivation: Latin double -nn- evolved into Spanish palatal ñ (written with a tilde, originally a tiny n drawn above the first n!).

hambre.context_translation: I am very hungry (lit. I have much hunger).
hambre.etymology_derivation: Feminine noun (mucha hambre) that takes el in the singular like el agua, and shows f- → h- from Latin famēs!

razón.context_translation: You are completely right (lit. You have all the reason).
razón.etymology_derivation: To be right in Spanish is to 'have reason': tienes razón.

lunes.etymology_derivation: Spanish uses the masculine article el/los to mean 'on [weekday]': el lunes ('on Monday'), los lunes ('on Mondays')!

martes.context_translation: We'll see each other on Tuesday.

miércoles.etymology_derivation: Mercury's day, with an esdrújula accent.

viernes.etymology_derivation: Venus's day. All five (lunes–viernes) end in -es and stay unchanged in the plural (el lunes / los lunes)!

sábado.context_translation: On Saturday we're going to the movies.

semana.context_translation: This week I have a lot of work.

enero.etymology_derivation: Months take en ('in'): en enero, en mayo.

he.etymology_derivation: Latin habēre split into tener (possession: tengo un coche) and haber (auxiliary: he hablado, plus hay)!

has.etymology_derivation: Never separate haber from its participle!

hablado.etymology_derivation: Past participles after haber NEVER change for gender or number — always end in -o!

hecho.english_meaning: done, made (participle of hacer); fact (el hecho)
hecho.shift_rule: Double sound shift: factum → hecho (f→h AND ct→ch!)
hecho.etymology_derivation: Look at Latin factum → Spanish hecho: initial f- became silent h-, AND medial -ct- became -ch-!

visto.etymology_derivation: You already know it from 'Hasta la vista'!

hablé.context_translation: Yesterday I spoke with my mother.
hablé.etymology_derivation: Notice how the accent mark carries the entire tense difference: hablo ('I speak') vs. habló ('he/she spoke')!

comí.context_translation: Yesterday I ate at that restaurant.

fue.english_cognate: was / went (shared preterite of ser & ir!)
fue.shift_rule: Shared preterite of ser and ir (fui, fuiste, fue)
fue.etymology_derivation: ser ('to be') and ir ('to go') share the exact same preterite forms: fui ('I was / I went'), fue ('it was / he went')!

hablaba.english_meaning: I / he / she was speaking, used to speak
hablaba.context_phrase: Cuando vivía allí, hablaba español todos los días.
hablaba.context_translation: When I lived there, I spoke Spanish every day.
hablaba.etymology_derivation: Every -ar verb takes -aba in the imperfect with zero irregulars!

era.english_meaning: I / he / she / it was (imperfect of ser)
era.context_phrase: Cuando era joven, vivía en Madrid.
era.context_translation: When I was young, I lived in Madrid.
era.etymology_derivation: Latin erat — English 'era' (an ongoing epoch of time) is the exact same root!

estaba.english_meaning: I / he / she / it was (imperfect of estar)

desde.context_phrase: Vivo aquí desde hace tres años.
desde.context_translation: I have lived here for three years.
desde.etymology_derivation: Just like French depuis, ongoing actions in Spanish stay in the PRESENT tense with desde hace (or hace X que + present)!

más.english_meaning: more, most (with accent; mas without accent = 'but')
más.context_phrase: Madrid es más grande que Toledo.
más.etymology_derivation: más... que = 'more... than'; el/la más... = 'the most / -est'.

menos.context_phrase: Es menos caro que el hotel.
menos.context_translation: It is less expensive than the hotel.

mejor.context_phrase: Este vino es mejor que ese.
mejor.context_translation: This wine is better than that one.

tan.context_translation: It is as important as that.

como.etymology_derivation: Unaccented como closes equality comparisons: tan... como.

me.etymology_derivation: Walks left of conjugated verbs or hooks onto infinitives.

nos.english_meaning: us, to us, ourselves, each other

le.english_cognate: to him, to her, to usted (dative)
le.english_meaning: to him, to her, to you (usted) (plural: les)
le.shift_rule: Indirect object pronoun (becomes se before lo/la!)
le.context_phrase: Le doy el libro a María.
le.context_translation: I give the book to María.
le.etymology_derivation: Gender-neutral indirect object ('to him / to her / to usted'); turns into se before lo/la/los/las (Se lo doy)!

se.english_meaning: himself, herself, yourself (usted), themselves; to him/her/them (before lo/la)
se.shift_rule: Reflexive AND the 'se lo' replacement for *le lo
se.context_translation: I tell it to him/her today.
se.etymology_derivation: Whenever le or les meets lo/la/los/las, Spanish softens the tongue-twister *le lo into se lo!

dar.context_translation: I'll give it to you now.
dar.etymology_derivation: Latin dare — English donate and data ('things given').

decir.english_meaning: to say, to tell (digo: I say/tell)
decir.shift_rule: Latin dīcere (-go verb: digo, dices, dice)
decir.etymology_derivation: Latin dīcere — English dictate, diction, predict.

saber.english_meaning: to know (facts, information, how to do something; sé: I know)
saber.context_translation: I know how to speak Spanish.
saber.etymology_derivation: Used for facts, clauses, and skills (sé + bare infinitive, without 'cómo').

conocer.english_meaning: to know, be familiar with (people, places; conozco: I know)
conocer.shift_rule: 1st sg in -zco: conozco (takes personal 'a' before people!)
conocer.context_phrase: Conozco Madrid y conozco a tu hermano.
conocer.context_translation: I know Madrid and I know your brother.
conocer.etymology_derivation: Before a specific person, conhecer ALWAYS requires the personal 'a': conozco a María!

levantarse.english_meaning: to get up (me levanto: I get up)
levantarse.context_translation: I get up at seven o'clock.

acostarse.english_meaning: to go to bed, lie down (me acuesto: I go to bed)
acostarse.etymology_derivation: From costa ('rib/side') = 'to lay oneself on one's side'.

gustar.english_meaning: to be pleasing to (me gusta: I like, lit. it pleases to me)
gustar.shift_rule: Inverted dative experiencer verb (gusta sg. / gustan pl.)
gustar.context_phrase: Me gusta el café y me gustan los libros.
gustar.context_translation: I like coffee and I like books.
gustar.etymology_derivation: Latin gustāre ('to taste') — English gusto and disgust. The thing liked is the grammatical SUBJECT!

gusta.english_meaning: pleases (me gusta + singular noun or infinitive)
gusta.etymology_derivation: With a plural noun, adds -n: me gustan las ciudades.

encantar.english_meaning: to love, be delighted by (me encanta: I love)
encantar.etymology_derivation: Literally 'it enchants me': me encanta (sg.), me encantan (pl.).

gustaría.english_cognate: would please (me gustaría: I would like)
gustaría.english_meaning: would please (conditional: me gustaría = I would like)
gustaría.context_translation: I would like to reserve a table.
gustaría.etymology_derivation: Every Spanish conditional simply glues -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían onto the whole infinitive!

ojalá.english_meaning: hopefully, I hope that, if only (always triggers subjunctive!)
ojalá.context_translation: I hope you have a great day!
ojalá.etymology_derivation: Direct Arabic inheritance in Spanish; always triggers the subjunctive mood (tengas, venga, sea)!

hierro.shift_rule: Latin ferrum (f- → silent h- AND e → ie)
hierro.etymology_derivation: Look at both shifts firing together: Latin f- became silent h-, and stressed e became ie: ferrum → hierro!

lleno.etymology_derivation: Latin plēnus ('full', English plenty/replenish) shifted initial pl- to ll-: lleno!

poner.english_meaning: to put, to place (pongo: I put)
poner.shift_rule: Root of the -poner family (proponer, suponer, componer)
poner.context_phrase: Pongo el libro en la mesa.
poner.context_translation: I put the book on the table.
poner.etymology_derivation: Latin pōnere — root of propose, suppose, compose, expose.

proponer.context_translation: I propose an idea to you.
proponer.etymology_derivation: Conjugates identically to poner: propongo, propones, propuso, propuesto.

mantener.context_translation: I want to maintain the tradition.

obtener.context_translation: I want to obtain the confirmation.

mostrar.shift_rule: Boot verb o → ue (root of demostrar)
mostrar.context_translation: Will you show me the way?
mostrar.etymology_derivation: Highlighted in Language Transfer: mostrar ('to show') and demostrar ('to demonstrate/prove') share the exact same o → ue boot!

traer.context_translation: Will you bring me the bill, please?
traer.etymology_derivation: Latin trahere ('to pull/draw', English tractor, attract, distract).

estación.etymology_derivation: Covers both 'train station' and 'season of the year'.

tren.context_phrase: Tomo el tren a las ocho.
tren.context_translation: I take the train at eight.

billete.etymology_derivation: un billete de ida y vuelta = 'a round-trip ticket'.

cuenta.etymology_derivation: The restaurant bill is literally 'the count' (la cuenta).

queso.etymology_derivation: Latin cāseus gave English 'casein' and Spanish queso.

música.etymology_derivation: Always takes the definite article after gustar: me gusta la música.

cine.context_translation: Let's go to the movies tonight.
cine.etymology_derivation: Masculine: el cine (a + el = al cine).

cabeza.context_translation: My head hurts / I have a headache.
cabeza.etymology_derivation: Used inside el rompecabezas ('the head-breaker' = jigsaw puzzle).

mano.etymology_derivation: Just as el día and el problema are masculine in -a, la mano ('the hand', from Latin feminine manus) is the famous feminine noun ending in -o!

corazón.etymology_derivation: Latin cor ('heart', English core/cordial) expanded into corazón.

abrigo.shift_rule: From abrigar 'to shelter from the cold'
abrigo.context_translation: I am wearing a black coat.
abrigo.etymology_derivation: llevar ('to carry/wear') is used for wearing clothes.

vestido.etymology_derivation: Related to English vest and vestment.

cion.name: The -CIÓN Passport
cion.phonetic_rule: English -tion /-(e)ʃən/ becomes Spanish -ción /-ˈθjon/. Always stressed on the ó, and 100% feminine (la).
cion.historical_linguistics: Descends from Latin third-declension abstract nouns in -tiō (accusative -tiōnem). English borrowed thousands via French; Spanish evolved -ción directly.
cion.philological_note: Because every single -ción noun is feminine, this family hands you grammatical gender for thousands of words without memorization.

dad.name: The -DAD Quality Bridge
dad.phonetic_rule: English abstract nouns in -ty correspond to Spanish -dad /-ˈdað/. 100% feminine (la).
dad.historical_linguistics: From Latin abstract quality nouns in -tās, accusative -tātem. Spanish lenited the intervocalic dental stop to -dad.
dad.philological_note: City (ciudad), reality (realidad), university (universidad). The ending guarantees feminine gender.

mente.name: The -MENTE Adverb Engine
mente.phonetic_rule: Feminine adjective + -mente /-ˈmente/ forms adverbs corresponding to English -ly.
mente.historical_linguistics: Originates from the Latin ablative phrase [adjective] mente ('with a ... mind'). Because mens is feminine in Latin, Spanish preserves the feminine adjective stem.
mente.philological_note: Notice how Spanish preserves the feminine form: exactamente (not exactomente). If the base adjective carries a tilde, it keeps it: fácilmente.

ar_engine.name: The -ar Verb Factory
ar_engine.phonetic_rule: English Latinate nouns in -ation correspond to Spanish first-conjugation infinitives in -ar /-ˈaɾ/.
ar_engine.historical_linguistics: Latin first-conjugation verbs in -āre. English borrowed the noun form; Spanish kept the verb stem alive.
ar_engine.philological_note: The 'celebrar trap': strip the entire -ation before attaching -ar. Celebración → celebrar (not celebratar).

ico.name: The -ICO Bridge
ico.phonetic_rule: English adjectives in -ic / -ical correspond to Spanish -ico /-iko/ (masculine) / -ica (feminine). Always carries a written accent on the antepenultimate syllable.
ico.historical_linguistics: Greek -ikos passed through Latin -icus. In Spanish, these are palabras esdrújulas and must be written with a tilde.
ico.philological_note: Mágico, público, básico, económico, romántico. The tilde tells your voice exactly where to jump.

al.name: The -AL Invariable Passport
al.phonetic_rule: English adjectives ending in -al match Spanish -al /-ˈal/ with identical spelling and gender-invariable singular form.
al.historical_linguistics: Latin adjectival suffix -ālis ('pertaining to'). Both languages kept the spelling; Spanish stresses the final syllable.
al.philological_note: El plan natural, la idea natural: no gender change in the singular.

f_to_h.name: Latin F- ➔ Silent H-
f_to_h.phonetic_rule: Latin initial f- weakened into an aspiration and became completely silent h- in Spanish, while English kept the Latin f- cognate.
f_to_h.historical_linguistics: Castilian contact with Basque/Cantabrian substrate languages lacking initial /f/ caused Latin /f-/ to weaken into silent h-.
f_to_h.philological_note: Hacer ↔ fact/manufacture; hijo ↔ filial; hierro ↔ ferrous; horno ↔ furnace. When you see a silent h-, think f.

ct_to_ch.name: Latin -CT- ➔ Spanish -CH-
ct_to_ch.phonetic_rule: Latin medial -ct- palatalized into Spanish -ch- /-tʃ-, while English kept the learned Latin -ct- form.
ct_to_ch.historical_linguistics: The velar stop /k/ vocalized into a palatal glide [j] which then fused with the dental /t/ into the affricate /tʃ/.
ct_to_ch.philological_note: Noctem ➔ noche (nocturnal); lactem ➔ leche (lactose); factum ➔ hecho (fact); octō ➔ ocho (octave).

pl_cl_fl_to_ll.name: Latin PL-/CL-/FL- ➔ Spanish LL-
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.phonetic_rule: Latin initial consonant clusters pl-, cl-, fl- palatalized into Spanish ll- /ʎ/ (or /ʝ/).
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.historical_linguistics: The initial stop or fricative conditioned progressive palatalization of the liquid /l/ in Western Iberian Vulgar Latin.
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.philological_note: Clāmāre ➔ llamar (claim/clamor); clāvis ➔ llave (clef/clavicle); pluvia ➔ lluvia (pluvial); plēnus ➔ lleno (plenty).

compounds.lore: rascar 'to scrape' + cielos 'skies'. Spanish verb-object compound, invariably masculine singular.
parar 'to ward off' + aguas 'waters'. Rainfall is conceptualized as plural precipitation.
abrir 'to open' + latas 'cans'. Spanish names tools as active verbs doing work on plural objects.

compounds.example_translation: The park ranger cares for nature.

compounds.lore: A recursive compound: limpiar ('to clean') attached to parabrisas ('ward-off-breezes').
romper 'to break' + cabezas 'heads'. A riddle so difficult it threatens to crack your skull.
cumplir 'to fulfill/complete' + años 'years'. A Spanish birthday celebrates completing another annual cycle.
matar 'to kill' + moscas 'flies'. Blunt teleological naming.
tragar 'to swallow/devour' + monedas 'coins'. Folk satire naming the casino machine.
girar 'to turn/revolve' (gyrate) + sol 'sun' (solar). The flower named for turning its face toward the sun.
salvar 'to save' + vidas 'lives'. Identical verb-object blueprint to English lifesaver.
compounds.example_sentence: El salvavidas está en la playa.
compounds.example_translation: The lifeguard is on the beach.

compounds.lore: espantar 'to frighten/scare' + pájaros 'birds'. Exact calque of English scarecrow.
compounds.example_sentence: Hay un espantapájaros en el jardín.
compounds.example_translation: There is a scarecrow in the garden.

compounds.lore: parar 'to stop/ward off' + brisas 'breezes' — the base inside limpiaparabrisas.

falseFriends.trap_note: actualmente refers to time, not fact. 'Actually' is en realidad or de hecho.
embarazada means pregnant! If you are embarrassed, say avergonzado or apenado.
la librería sells books; the lending library is la biblioteca.
falseFriends.example_sentence: Compré la novela en la librería.
falseFriends.example_translation: I bought the novel at the bookstore.

falseFriends.trap_note: asistir a una reunión means to attend it, not to help. Assisting is ayudar.
falseFriends.example_translation: I am going to attend the concert.

falseFriends.trap_note: éxito means success or triumph. The physical doorway or exit is la salida.
recordar means to remember (call back to the heart). Recording audio or video is grabar.
sensible means having deep feelings or sensitive skin. A sensible, level-headed person is sensato.
falseFriends.example_translation: He is a very sensitive artist.

falseFriends.trap_note: la sopa is soup you eat with a spoon! Soap for washing is el jabón.
estar constipado means having a common nasal cold. Constipated is estreñido.
falseFriends.example_translation: I have a cough and a head cold.

falseFriends.trap_note: la carpeta is a document folder or binder. Floor carpet is la alfombra.
falseFriends.example_sentence: Guarda los papeles en la carpeta.
falseFriends.example_translation: Keep the papers in the folder.

falseFriends.trap_note: la fábrica is an industrial manufacturing plant. Textile fabric is la tela.
falseFriends.example_sentence: Trabaja en una fábrica de coches.
falseFriends.example_translation: He works in a car factory.

falseFriends.trap_note: pretender means to intend or aim for something. Feigning or pretending is fingir.
falseFriends.example_translation: I do not intend to offend you.

falseFriends.trap_note: soportar means to bear weight or tolerate emotionally. Supporting someone is apoyar.
Historically, bizarro meant brave and gallant in Spanish. Strange or bizarre is raro or extraño.
realizar means to make something real (carry out a project). Realizing a fact in your head is darse cuenta de ('to give oneself account of').
falseFriends.example_translation: We are going to carry out the project.

falseFriends.trap_note: la lectura is the act of reading a book. A university lecture is una conferencia or una clase.
el delito is a crime or legal offense (cousin of delinquent)! Delight is el deleite or la delicia.
tengo un compromiso means 'I have a prior commitment/obligation' (or wedding engagement). A mutual concession is un acuerdo.
falseFriends.example_translation: Today I have a family commitment.
